We've seen multiple examples of why granting Meta's Muse app "Full Disk Access" to your Mac is a terrible idea, and another major privacy issue has just been discovered. Muse has been found to be analysing your communications with everyone in your life every hour.

Apple's concern over this development is justified, and the company said in a blog post that it will introduce additional controls for the "Full Disk Access" feature that has been fuelling the problem.

Meta's Muse app has made things urgent

Meta recently launched its Muse Personal AI Agent smart assistant for iPhone and Mac. Despite granting a Meta app unfettered access to all your Apple devices being clearly inadvisable, the app quickly shot to the top of the App Store charts.

Predictably, things soon started going seriously wrong. And things haven't improved since — *Wired* reports that security researcher Karan Joshi found that Meta has instructed Muse to extract all the information needed to build a complete map of all your relationships.

One of Muse's instructions appears to give it the ability to "build a profile page for every person in the user's life." This hourly process involves collecting data on family members, partners, friends, colleagues, "collaborators," and people you "follow," and the instructions say: "where they live, what they do, recurring topics (moving, shared savings goals)," the instructions say. It adds that the model can record "important dates" like birthdays or anniversaries. A person's experiences might include backstory like "a March trip, a resolved argument, last week's milestone."

Apple tightens up Full Disk Access

You might think that a prompt asking for "Full Disk Access" to your Mac is self-explanatory, but apparently not. Even tech-savvy people have granted this all-access pass to their computer without realising just how dangerous a step it is.

Apple says the feature was originally intended for backup apps, but developers have since been using it for much more, including AI smart assistants. The company has said it intends to "introduce additional controls" to make sure users fully understand what they're doing when they grant this permission.

What Apple must and must not do

Apple says this step is "critically important," and I entirely agree. When the existing permission request clearly fails to fully convey the gravity of granting this access, Apple must make sure users truly understand what they're allowing.

I'd love to see much more explicit wording, advising people not to do it unless they're sure they understand the consequences. Something along these lines:

Basically, no wording can be too strong. I'd also welcome a one-time confirmation for apps that have already been granted this access.

Peter — Most Liked Comment

While I find Apple's periodic confirmation of whether I want to continue granting location permission to an app a little annoying, I do appreciate the design. There was one occasion when I realised I no longer wanted a particular app to have that level of access. It also reminds me to think regularly about which apps might be using my location.

However, Apple must absolutely not repeat the mistake it made with screen recording on macOS Sequoia. That's certainly equally dangerous in its own way, and a strong warning is appropriate, but what Apple did at the time was force us to confirm these permissions weekly and every time we rebooted.

This was widely criticised as turning macOS into Microsoft Vista, and imposing a "subscription you didn't buy and can't cancel." In my eyes, Apple's occasional repeated permission requests on iPhone already go too far in this direction. For example, I've granted Citymapper access to my location so it can keep providing navigation in the background; no, Apple, I really don't need you to confirm whether I still want to do that.

Absolutely, issue the strongest possible warning about granting Full Disk Access, but if someone chooses to do so, macOS must accept their decision. Thanks, but no weekly or other regular mandatory confirmations.
